COD.hook: The Congo is the deepest river in the world, over 220m in places — and the country holds most of the world's cobalt.
COD.place: The vast heart of Africa astride the equator, with only a 40km squeeze of Atlantic coast.
COD.borders: King Leopold's personal 'Congo Free State', recognized at the 1885 Berlin Conference: the Congo basin's rivers and watersheds, plus the narrow corridor to the Atlantic at the river's mouth — the strip that cuts Angola's Cabinda off from Angola.

AGO.hook: Portuguese-speaking, and split in two — the oil-rich Cabinda exclave is cut off from the rest by a strip of DR Congo.
AGO.place: On the Atlantic below DR Congo, with the separate Cabinda enclave sitting to its north.
AGO.borders: Portugal's coastal colony pushed inland to Berlin-Conference-era lines; Cabinda sits detached to the north because Leopold's Congo was granted a corridor to the sea between the two in 1885.

TCD.hook: Lake Chad has lost about 90% of its surface area since the 1960s — the country is named after a lake that is nearly gone.
TCD.place: Landlocked in north-central Africa, running from deep Sahara down into the Sahel.
TCD.borders: French Equatorial Africa's desert north: straight survey lines with Libya — the Aouzou Strip was confirmed Chadian by the world court in 1994 — and a Lake Chad boundary drawn when the lake was far larger than it is now.

CMR.hook: Called Africa in miniature — desert, rainforest, savanna, mountains and coast in one country, with both English and French official.
CMR.place: At the crook of the Gulf of Guinea, where West Africa turns the corner and heads south.
CMR.borders: German Kamerun split between Britain and France after WWI, then partly reunited by ballot: in 1961 the British north voted to join Nigeria and the British south to join Cameroon; the world court added Bakassi in a ruling completed in 2008.

SSD.hook: The newest country in the world, independent in 2011 — and the Sudd wetland at its centre is among the largest on Earth.
SSD.place: Landlocked below Sudan, between Ethiopia and the Central African Republic.
SSD.borders: The internal north–south administrative line of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, made an international border by the 2011 independence referendum — with Abyei's status and several stretches of the line still unresolved.

CAF.hook: Sits almost exactly at the geographic centre of the continent, and is among the least visited countries on the planet.
CAF.place: Landlocked in the middle of Africa, below Chad and above DR Congo.
CAF.borders: France's Ubangi-Shari, a colony of administrative convenience linking French Congo to Chad: the Ubangi and Mbomou rivers draw the southern border, survey lines the rest.

COG.hook: Its capital Brazzaville faces Kinshasa across the river — the closest pair of capital cities anywhere in the world.
COG.place: On the Atlantic west of DR Congo. This is the smaller Congo; the two stare at each other across the water.
COG.borders: French Congo's share of the Berlin-era carve-up: the Congo and Ubangi rivers divide it from the vastly larger Belgian (now Democratic Republic of the) Congo — leaving Brazzaville and Kinshasa, the world's closest capitals, facing each other across the water.

GAB.hook: About 88% forest, and in 2002 it turned a tenth of the entire country into national parks in a single stroke.
GAB.place: On the equator on the Atlantic coast, below Cameroon and west of the Republic of the Congo.
GAB.borders: French Equatorial Africa's coastal quarter, divided from Congo along administrative lines; the northern boundary comes from the 1900 Franco-Spanish convention, with the offshore Mbanié islets dispute settled at the world court only in 2025.

GNQ.hook: The only African country with Spanish as an official language — and its capital is not on the mainland but on an island.
GNQ.place: A mainland slice plus islands in the Gulf of Guinea; Malabo sits on Bioko, closer to Cameroon than to its own territory.
GNQ.borders: Spain's two-part colony: the Rio Muni box on the mainland, drawn by the 1900 convention with France, plus Bioko island far offshore to the northwest — the capital sits on the island, most of the territory on the mainland, nothing contiguous.

STP.hook: Two volcanic islands on the equator that were once the largest cocoa producer in the world — from almost nothing to first place and back.
STP.place: In the Gulf of Guinea off Gabon, straddling the equator.
STP.borders: Two volcanic islands, uninhabited until Portuguese sugar planters arrived in the 1470s — the state is simply the islands, and no land border has ever existed.
